clue.text: Exhaust Caucasian talking like Spooner?

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don whose tongue traded the opening sounds of two neighbouring words, so a clue talking his way asks you to trade them back

parts.note: a Caucasian is a pale type, and the P and the T at the fronts of those two words change places

explanation.surface: Somebody wearing out a white man who insists on talking in the Reverend's muddled fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust' looks like the verb the surface is built on and is a car part instead. Say 'pale type' aloud and swap the two opening sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's exhaust system ends in the tailpipe at the back, and the pipe has given its name to the whole thing.

clue.text: Deer hunter set up equipment

indicators.note: In a down clue something set up has been stood on its end, so the letters are read from the bottom of the entry upwards

parts.note: an elk is the big deer of the northern forests
a cat hunts for a living, from the kitchen mouser to the lion

explanation.surface: A man who stalks deer laying out his gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deer hunter' is one person on the surface and two animals underneath. The equipment wanted is an angler's: tackle is rods, lines and hooks, and a tackle shop sells nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackle is the collective word for the gear a trade needs — the angler's rods, a ship's ropes and blocks — so it is equipment itself.

clue.text: Irruption from broken drain, nothing to stop it

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart, and letters that have come apart do not go back in the order they were printed
To stop a gap is to plug it, so the round letter is pushed into the middle of what has just been broken up

parts.note: the five letters of DRAIN in a new order
the round letter is what a scoreboard writes for nothing

explanation.surface: A cracked drainpipe with nothing in the way to hold the water back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing to stop it' does two jobs at once, naming a letter and saying where it goes. An inroad is a raid across somebody's border before it is anything as mild as progress.
explanation.definitionFit: An irruption is a violent breaking in, and an inroad is the raid itself — a force pushing across somebody else's border.

clue.text: Decorated parts of large garden, fencing apart

definitions.note: Paintwork is a collective singular — every painted surface of a house or a car counted as one thing — which is why the definition can be plural.

indicators.note: A fence is put round the outside of a plot, so the word doing the fencing closes round what follows it

parts.note: a park is a garden on the grand scale, laid out for a town or a country house
something pulled apart is in two, and the two words run together as five letters

explanation.surface: A big garden whose ornamental beds are kept separate by fencing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorated parts' sounds horticultural and means the painted surfaces of a house or a car. 'Apart' has to be heard as two words before it will give up its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Paintwork is the painted surface of a car or a building taken as a whole — the parts that carry the decoration and nothing else.

clue.text: Max intensity from little dog you can hear

indicators.note: What you can hear is the sound of a word and not its spelling, so the letters wanted are the ones that make the same noise

parts.note: a Peke is a Pekingese, the small flat-faced lapdog bred for the Chinese court

explanation.surface: A small yappy dog just within earshot.
explanation.walkthrough: Peke is the everyday British short form of Pekingese and is said exactly like the answer. The definition is the crest of a graph or a fever, not a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: A fever, a demand or a rush hour is at its peak when it is at its most intense, the highest point the thing reaches.

clue.text: Large bear coming over, American's fair game

indicators.note: Something coming over has turned right over on the way, so the letters in front of the phrase arrive back to front

parts.note: L is the size printed on a clothing label
Winnie-the-Pooh is the bear a crossword reaches for first
A is the standard shortening of American

explanation.surface: A big bear dropping in on an American who reckons it is legitimate quarry.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal swallows the size letter as well as the bear, which is why the answer's hyphen falls where no word does. Hoop-la is the stall where you toss rings over prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoop-la is the ring-tossing stall of a British funfair, so a game belonging to the fair is what the answer is.

clue.text: Tiny amount of elasticity saving billions

indicators.note: Saving here is the old sense 'except for', so what comes after it is the part left out rather than the part kept

parts.note: the elasticity of a ball is its bounce
b is the abbreviation for billions, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A cost-cutting exercise of enormous size that still leaves some spring in the figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' reads as thrift and is a deletion instruction, which is what makes the economy drive of the surface so convincing. An ounce of sense is the proverbial smallest quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is a sixteenth of a pound, and in phrases like 'an ounce of truth' it stands for the least amount there could be.

clue.text: In favour of friend consuming no alcohol

parts.note: to be pro something is to be in favour of it

indicators.note: To consume something is to take it inside you, so the word in front opens up and swallows what comes next

parts.note: a pal is a friend
the two letters of the word itself, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: Sticking up for a friend who touches no alcohol at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No alcohol' is split down the middle: the first word is wordplay and the second is the definition. Propanol is rubbing alcohol, an alcohol to a chemist and undrinkable to anybody else.
explanation.definitionFit: Propanol is one of the simple alcohols of chemistry, the three-carbon member of the series that starts with methanol and ethanol.

clue.text: Emperor's son expected to embrace king after bow

indicators.note: An embrace closes the arms round somebody, so the word doing it takes the letter beside it inside

parts.note: a bow built in stone is an arch

indicators.note: What comes after something follows it, so the embracing pair is written behind the piece named at the end of the clue

parts.note: a train expected at six is due at six
K is the king on a chessboard and in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A prince who is expected to bow before he hugs his monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' is the shape, not the movement the surface stages, and the last word of the clue is the first piece of the answer. An archduke was a prince of the Austrian imperial house.
explanation.definitionFit: The Habsburg emperors gave the title archduke to the princes of their own house, so an emperor's son held it by birth.

clue.text: Maybe envy what the Sistine Chapel has during conclave?

parts.note: to elect a pope the cardinals are shut into the Sistine Chapel, so they are what it has
for as long as the conclave lasts they are in, locked under the Michelangelo ceiling until they agree

explanation.surface: The jealousy that might go round a chapel full of men waiting to elect a pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordplay and definition describe the same room: move the space one letter to the right and the answer becomes the chapel's occupants. Envy is one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: The seven deadly sins are also called the cardinal sins, and envy is one of the seven, which is what 'maybe' is owning up to.

clue.text: Careless make-up daughter has smeared

indicators.note: Letters smeared across a page run into one another, and what is smeared does not come out in the order it was laid down

parts.note: slap is British slang for make-up, from the theatre's greasepaint
d is the family-tree abbreviation for daughter
the three letters of HAS put down in another order

explanation.surface: A daughter who has put her make-up on in a rush and smudged it.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram hides inside 'has', a word so ordinary it reads as grammar rather than fodder. 'A bit of slap' is still how a British actor talks about the make-up box.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash work is done fast and without attention, so the tidying, checking and finishing a careless worker skips are exactly what it lacks.

clue.text: Horrible being stuck in Mallorca

indicators.note: Something stuck in a word is lodged inside it, so the letters are already sitting there in the order they are wanted

parts.note: three consecutive letters of MallORCa, taken without a single one moving

explanation.surface: A ghastly creature trapped on a Spanish holiday island.
explanation.walkthrough: Mallorca is the Spanish spelling of Majorca, and a place name is the last word a solver frisks for a hidden answer. Orcs are the goblin foot-soldiers of Tolkien's evil armies.
explanation.definitionFit: An orc is the brutish goblin-warrior of Tolkien's books and the films made from them, about as horrible a being as fantasy has produced.

clue.text: Construction needing support, thin brace you'd say

parts.note: a lean man is a thin one

indicators.note: What you would say is the sound of a word, so the second piece is spelt the way it is heard and not the way it is meant

parts.note: a brace of pheasants is a pair of them, and the number said aloud is spelt differently

explanation.surface: A rickety building held up by a single slender strut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brace' looks like the very prop the construction needs and is the shooting man's pair instead. A lean-to has three walls of its own and borrows the fourth from the building it rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is the shed built against a house wall, propped on the bigger building because it has no fourth wall to stand on.

clue.text: In case of feud, one coach for club with two mugs?

definitions.note: The answer names a class of card and the definition describes one member of it — the club suit's king, queen or jack — with the question mark owning up to the example.

indicators.note: The case of a word is its outside, the two letters the rest travels in, and what follows is packed between them

parts.note: the first and last letters of FEUD, the case the middle of the word sits in
the ace is the one of its suit
a railway coach is a car

explanation.surface: One trainer hired to settle a quarrel at a club run by a pair of fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mugs' means faces here rather than fools, and a court card shows two of them because the picture is printed head to head against itself. Americans say face card where the British say court card.
explanation.definitionFit: A face card is a king, queen or jack, each drawn as a mirrored pair of heads, so the one in the club suit is a club with two mugs.

clue.text: Want good spring after poor

indicators.note: One thing after another follows it, so the piece named first in the clue is written second in this down entry

parts.note: mean soil is poor soil, thin and grudging
a well is a spring of water, sunk rather than found

explanation.surface: Hoping for a decent water supply after a disappointing one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' and 'mean' meet in the sense of scanty, not penniless. The definition reads oddly until you hear it as wanting good for somebody rather than wanting good things.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean well is to intend somebody good however the attempt turns out, so wanting good for them is the whole of what it claims.

clue.text: Celebration permitted after boys made new national record

indicators.note: Letters made new are made again, and letters made again come out in an arrangement other than the printed one
What is placed after something goes behind it, so the two letters for permitted end up at the back instead of where the clue prints them

parts.note: a do is British for any party laid on
the eight letters of BOYS MADE in another order
a thing OK'd has been permitted

explanation.surface: Boys throwing a party they were allowed once they had set a new national record.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'permitted' travels: everything else is built where the clue prints it. The Domesday Book is the survey of who held what land in England that William the Conqueror ordered in 1086.
explanation.definitionFit: The Domesday Book set down every manor, plough and villager in Norman England, and the nation has kept it as its founding record ever since.

clue.text: Animals that are one sort sing early

indicators.note: To sort a heap is to go through it and put it in an arrangement of your choosing, which is what happens to the letters beside it

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Creatures of a particular kind that start the dawn chorus before the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' sits between 'one' and 'sing' where it reads as a kind of animal rather than an instruction. The age itself is left unsaid — the definition counts the years and leaves you to name them.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearling is a beast that has lived a year — the word the racing and farming worlds use for colts, calves and lambs of that age.

clue.text: While gas sold regularly, using it?

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval, every second one, instead of all of them

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of GAS SOLD
'it' is the gas, and a vehicle running on gas is using it

explanation.surface: Fuel is on sale week after week and drivers keep burning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' can start from the second letter as fairly as the first, and here it does. The second piece keeps the same subject, so the whole clue stays about gas from end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: While and as long as both mean 'for the time that' — stay while you like and stay as long as you like are the same invitation.

clue.text: Detective Murphy listened to chief

indicators.note: What is listened to is taken in by ear, so the words in front are spelt as they sound rather than as they are written

parts.note: a dick is a detective in the American thrillers, and a murphy is a potato, a tater

explanation.surface: A policeman of that name paying close attention to his boss.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy for potato is Irish-English, the commonest surname standing in for the commonest crop. The capital letter makes it look like the detective's name, which is the one thing it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictator is the single man in charge with nobody above him to answer to, which is 'chief' taken to its limit.

clue.text: Very neat, smooth bridge broken by sharp hammer

indicators.note: A thing broken by something has had it driven into it, so the tool named at the end of the clue lands inside the letters in front

parts.note: to sand a board is to smooth it
the span is the arch a bridge throws between its piers
a pick is the hammer with a spike on it, swung at rock and ice

explanation.surface: A polished bridge smashed open by a workman swinging a pointed hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' is the carpenter's verb, not the adjective the surface offers, and the insertion falls one letter into the first word rather than at the join. A spick was once a nail and a span a fresh-cut chip.
explanation.definitionFit: A spick and span kitchen has been cleaned and put straight until nothing is out of place, which is neatness at full stretch.

clue.text: Disgraceful mark idiots picked up on degree course

indicators.note: In a down clue something picked up is lifted back the way it came, so those letters read upwards
In a down entry one thing on another rests above it, so the lifted letters go in at the top

parts.note: a git is British slang for a contemptible fool
an MA is the master's degree, and the course is the one that leads to it

explanation.surface: Fools on a university course who have acquired a shameful reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' reads as acquiring a reputation and is the turnaround instruction instead. A stigma was first the brand burnt into a slave or a criminal, and only later the shame without the iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is the mark of disgrace that sticks to a person or a condition, so the definition is the word's literal sense laid out.

clue.text: 5 years in prison and losing heart

definitions.note: The definition counts out a quantity of years and the answer is the single noun for the set of them, so a plural clues a singular.

indicators.note: The heart of a word is the letter at its centre, and a word that loses it is written without it

parts.note: to be pent is to be shut up, the sense that survives in pent-up
AND with its middle letter N taken out

explanation.surface: Half a decade behind bars, with the will to carry on draining away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing heart' carries the whole misery of the surface and is only an instruction to drop a middle letter. A pentad is any group of five, and five years is the group the definition picks.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentad is a set of five of anything, and the word is used of a five-year span in particular, as a decade is used of ten.

clue.text: Motorcyclist worried route keeps clear?

indicators.note: A worried person turns a thing over and over, and letters worried at will not stay in the order they came in
What keeps something holds on to it inside itself, so the shuffled letters close round the piece that follows

parts.note: the five letters of ROUTE in a new order
to clear a house of mice is to rid it of them

explanation.surface: A motorcyclist fretting about whether the road ahead has been cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'clear' is wanted as a verb, not the adjective the surface hands you. An outrider is the police motorcyclist who rides ahead of a convoy holding the traffic back.
explanation.definitionFit: An outrider escorts a procession from in front or alongside, and on British roads that rider is on a motorcycle every time.

clue.text: Problem remains with unfinished canal

indicators.note: What is unfinished stops short of its end, so the name that follows hands over everything but its last letter

parts.note: what remains is what still is, the verb in its plainest form
the Suez Canal with its final letter left off

explanation.surface: A half-dug waterway that is still causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Suez is the canal a crossword wants whenever three of its four letters are needed. 'Remains' looks like the noun the surface needs and is a verb doing plain duty.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a matter causing difficulty — 'I have an issue with that' is the current way of saying there is a problem.

clue.text: Carefree British drunk male

parts.note: B is the shortening used on forms and team sheets for British
somebody lit, or lit up, has had a great deal to drink
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A cheerful drunk Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' is the word every solver reads as a shuffle instruction, and here it simply defines three letters. Blithe means light-hearted, though 'blithely' now hints at not noticing the damage.
explanation.definitionFit: A blithe spirit goes through the day light-hearted and untroubled, which is carefree with the worry taken out.

clue.text: Opponent learning code bored by books

indicators.note: To bore a thing is to drill through it, so what follows goes into the middle of the letters in front

parts.note: AI is the machine-learning code that trains itself on data
NT is the New Testament, the books a crossword means when it says books

explanation.surface: A student of programming bored stiff by the reading list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored by' is the reader's complaint on the surface and the drill's work underneath. An anti is a noun in its own right: the antis are the people campaigning against whatever is proposed.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti is somebody set against a cause and is the word the newspapers use for that side, so it names an opponent outright.

clue.text: Irritate chap, forgetting his name?

indicators.note: What is forgotten is not there, so the letter named after this word drops out of the word in front of it

parts.note: a gent is a chap
n is the abbreviation for name, and it is the letter the chap loses

explanation.surface: Annoying a man by failing to remember what he is called.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue acts out its own joke: the word for a man really does lose the letter that stands for his name. 'Get' in this sense is what a thing does when it gets to you.
explanation.definitionFit: When something gets to you it irritates you, and 'that really gets me' is the everyday way of saying so.

clue.text: Tinsel arrayed, almost time for this song?

definitions.text: Tinsel arrayed, almost time for this song?

indicators.note: To array a set of things is to set them out in whatever order you choose, so the letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the six letters of TINSEL set out in another order
nigh means almost, as in nigh on impossible
t is the physicist's symbol for time

explanation.surface: The decorations are up and Christmas Eve is very nearly here.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence does both jobs at once: it spells the carol out and states the occasion for singing it. 'Nigh' for almost is what lets the charade vanish into the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: with the tinsel hung it is nearly time for the carol Christmas Eve is built around, and that carol is the answer.

clue.text: Course ship's taken across lake

indicators.note: What is taken across something spans it from one side to the other, so the letters in front open out and sit on either side of what follows

parts.note: SS is the prefix on a steamship's name, as in SS Great Britain, and the apostrophe-s is the surface's 'has'
Erie is one of the Great Lakes, lying between Ontario and Ohio

explanation.surface: The route a steamer has taken across a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' is the ship's heading on the surface and something quite different in the definition. Erie is the Great Lake crosswords use because its four letters are the easiest to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: A course of lectures or of antibiotics is a set of them taken one after another, which is what a series is.

clue.text: Tree given dignified treatment after being cut?

parts.note: a fir is the evergreen of the northern woods
a staid person is sober and dignified, never seen to hurry

explanation.surface: A tree treated with great respect once it has been felled.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap in the answer falls inside the second word rather than between the two, which is what makes 'staid' disappear. The question mark covers the jump from a felled tree to a cut finger.
explanation.definitionFit: First aid is the treatment given on the spot to somebody just hurt, and a cut is the commonest reason the green box comes off the wall.
